blurb: Latin caput, head, gave chief, chef, captain, capital, cattle and kerchief (a cover-head); English head is probably a Germanic cousin.

meaning: to show, to point out; to pronounce
blurb: Latin dīcere, to say, gave verdict, dictionary, judge (one who speaks the law) and indicate; Germanic teach and token; Greek deiknynai, to show.
Old English wether (a yearling ram); Latin vetus, old, gave veteran and inveterate; vitulus, a yearling calf, probably gave veal and vellum.
Few and foal in Germanic; Latin pauper and pullus gave poor, poverty, pauper and poultry.
Yard, garden and girdle in Germanic; Latin hortus and cohors gave horticulture, cohort, court and courtesy.
Arm in Germanic; Latin ars and arma gave art, army, armada and alarm; Greek harmonia gave harmony.
Latin nāvis gave navy, naval, nave and navigate; Greek naus gave nautical, nausea (seasickness) and astronaut.
Latin salvus, solidus and salūs gave safe, save, salute, solid and soldier, one who served for a solid gold coin.
Feather in Germanic; Latin petere, to seek, gave appetite, petition, compete and repeat; Greek pteron, wing, gave helicopter and pterodactyl.
Latin coquere gave cook, kitchen, cuisine, biscuit (twice-cooked) and precocious (ripened early); Greek peptein gave peptic.
Latin crēscere and creāre gave crescent, croissant, increase, create, concrete and recruit; Ceres, goddess of grain, gave cereal.
Get and forget via Old Norse; Latin prehendere gave prison, comprehend, apprentice, enterprise and entrepreneur.
Come in Germanic; Latin venīre gave adventure, avenue, convent, event, prevent, revenue and souvenir.
Latin villa and vīcus gave village, villain, vicinity and (through Old English wīc) the -wich of Norwich; Greek oikos, house, gave economy and ecology.
Wealth on the hoof: Old English feoh (fee); Latin pecū gave pecūnia, money — pecuniary, impecunious — and peculiar.
Latin dare and dōnum gave data, date, donate, pardon, render, tradition, treason and rendezvous; Greek dōron, gift, gave Dorothy and Theodore.
Else in Germanic; Latin alius, alter and ultrā gave alien, alias, alibi, alter, ultimate and outrage; Greek allos gave allegory.
Tug, tow and team in Germanic; Latin dūcere and dux gave duke, duct, educate, conduct, produce and seduce.
Latin candēre, to shine white, gave candle, candid, candidate, chandelier, incandescent and incense.
Latin īre, to go, gave exit, issue, ambition, itinerary, transit, initial and perish; also Old English ēode, “went”.
Wane and want in Germanic; Latin vacuus and vānus gave vacuum, vacation, vacant, vain, vanish and void.
Latin movēre gave move, motion, motor, emotion, moment, momentum, mobile and mob.
While in Germanic; Latin quiēs gave quiet, quit, quite, coy, acquit, tranquil and requiem.
Latin senex and senior gave senate, senile, senior, sire, sir and surly (once “sirly”, lordly); Irish sean, old.
Timber (once a building) in Germanic; Latin domus and dominus gave domestic, dome, dominion, danger and dungeon; Greek despotēs gave despot.
Strew and straw in Germanic; Latin sternere and struere gave street, stratum, structure, construct, destroy and instrument.
Ten in Germanic; Latin decem gave December, decimal, decimate, dean and dime; Greek deka gave decade.
Saw, scythe and sedge in Germanic; Latin secāre gave section, segment, sector, insect, dissect and sickle.

meaning: to lead across, to pass over
blurb: Ford, fare and fjord in Germanic; Latin portus and porta gave port, portal, porch, opportunity and importune.
